questions.question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.fun_fact: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood to the gills, and the third pumps it to the rest of the body. The main heart stops beating when the octopus swims — which is why they prefer crawling.

questions.question: How long can a Greenland shark live?
questions.fun_fact: The Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate known to science. A landmark 2016 study estimated one individual at around 392 years old (±120), making 400 years the best-supported upper estimate. They reach sexual maturity at around 150 years old.

questions.question: Which animal sleeps only about 2 hours per day?
questions.fun_fact: Giraffes sleep an average of just 1.9 hours a day, often in short 5-minute naps. They rarely lie down because getting back up takes too long and leaves them vulnerable.

questions.question: Which insect can pull 850 times its own body weight?
questions.fun_fact: The horned dung beetle (Onthophagus taurus) is the world's strongest animal relative to its weight. That's equivalent to a human pulling six fully loaded double-decker buses.

questions.question: Which animal has the highest blood pressure of any living creature?
questions.fun_fact: Giraffes have a blood pressure of around 280/180 mmHg — twice that of humans. Their heart weighs up to 12 kg and must pump blood almost 2 metres up to the brain.

questions.question: How do elephants communicate over long distances?

answers.text: Through infrasound vibrations in the ground
Through chemical signals in the air

questions.fun_fact: Elephants produce infrasound waves that travel through the ground and are detected by other elephants through their feet. They can communicate over distances of up to 32 kilometres.

questions.question: Which bird can fly backwards?
questions.fun_fact: Hummingbirds are the only birds capable of sustained backwards flight. Their wings beat up to 80 times per second, and their heart beats over 1,200 times per minute.

questions.question: Which animal can change sex during its lifetime?
questions.fun_fact: All clownfish are born male. The dominant female leads the group — if she dies, the top-ranking male transforms into a female. This means Nemo would have become Nemo's new mum.

questions.question: Which land animal has the longest pregnancy?
questions.fun_fact: African elephants are pregnant for nearly two years — the longest gestation of any land mammal. The calf already weighs around 100 kg at birth.

questions.question: Which plant is considered the fastest-growing in the world?
questions.fun_fact: Certain bamboo species can grow up to 91 cm per day — almost 1 cm per hour. You can literally watch bamboo grow.

questions.question: Which animal uses tools to open shells?
questions.fun_fact: Sea otters lie on their backs, balance a rock on their chest and smash shellfish against it. Each otter has a favourite stone, which it stores in a skin pouch under its arm.

questions.question: How many eyes does a bee have?
questions.fun_fact: Bees have five eyes: two large compound eyes on the sides of their head and three small simple eyes (ocelli) on top, which measure light intensity and polarisation.

questions.question: Which animal can run on water?
questions.fun_fact: The basilisk lizard, also called the 'Jesus Christ lizard', can run across water at up to 1.5 metres per second. Specialised skin flaps on its hind feet create air pockets beneath the surface.

questions.question: How many teeth can a shark produce in its lifetime?
questions.fun_fact: Sharks have a conveyor belt of teeth: new rows constantly grow behind existing ones. A single shark can produce over 30,000 teeth in its lifetime.

questions.question: Which tree species includes the oldest known individual non-clonal tree?
questions.fun_fact: The oldest known bristlecone pine, named 'Methuselah', in California is over 4,850 years old. Its exact location is kept secret to protect it from vandalism.

questions.question: Which animal can survive for weeks without its head?
questions.fun_fact: A cockroach can live for weeks without its head because it breathes through openings in its body and has a decentralised nervous system. It eventually dies of dehydration since it can't drink.

questions.question: How do dolphins sleep?

answers.text: With only one half of their brain
Only a few seconds at a time

questions.fun_fact: Dolphins practise 'unihemispheric sleep': one brain half sleeps while the other stays awake. This allows them to keep breathing and watch for predators — they literally sleep with one eye open.

questions.question: Which of these animals was the first known to have blue, copper-based blood?
questions.fun_fact: Horseshoe crab blood is copper-based rather than iron-based, making it blue. It is used in medicine to detect bacterial toxins in vaccines — a litre costs over €13,000.

questions.question: How far can a flea jump relative to its own body length?
questions.fun_fact: A flea can jump 150 times its own body length. Scaled to a human, that would be a jump of nearly 300 metres — the length of three football pitches.

questions.question: Which animal produces the strongest natural fibre?
questions.fun_fact: The silk of Darwin's bark spider is ten times stronger than Kevlar and the toughest known biological material. Its webs can span rivers and stretch up to 25 metres.

questions.question: Which animal has no stomach?
questions.fun_fact: Seahorses have no stomach — food passes straight through their intestine. This means they must eat almost constantly, consuming up to 3,000 tiny crustaceans per day.

questions.question: Which animal can see ultraviolet light?
questions.fun_fact: Reindeer can see UV light, which helps them in the Arctic winter. Predator urine and lichen (their food) stand out sharply against snow under UV light.

questions.question: How many legs does a woodlouse have?
questions.fun_fact: Woodlice have 14 legs and are not insects but crustaceans. They are among the few crustaceans to live entirely on land, breathing through pleopodal lungs on the underside of their abdomen.

questions.question: Which animal can lower its body temperature to nearly 0°C to survive winter?
questions.fun_fact: The Arctic ground squirrel drops its body temperature to as low as −2.9°C during hibernation — below freezing. It is the only mammal known to survive a sub-zero body temperature.

questions.question: Which fungus is the largest known organism on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: A honey fungus (Armillaria ostoyae) in Oregon covers 9 square kilometres underground and is estimated to be 2,400 years old. Its mycelium network is larger than 1,200 football pitches.

questions.question: Which animal has fingerprints nearly identical to human fingerprints?
questions.fun_fact: Koala fingerprints are so similar to human ones that they are almost indistinguishable even under a microscope. Koalas are not related to primates — the fingerprints evolved independently.

questions.question: Which animal can clone itself?
questions.fun_fact: The marbled crayfish reproduces exclusively through parthenogenesis — every individual is a genetic clone of its mother. The entire species likely descended from a single animal in a German aquarium in the 1990s.

questions.question: Which animal holds the record for the most legs ever counted on a single individual?
questions.fun_fact: Eumillipes persephone was discovered in Australia in 2021 and has up to 1,306 legs — the first animal to truly deserve the name 'millipede'.

questions.question: Which animal can regrow entire limbs, organs, and parts of its brain?
questions.fun_fact: The axolotl can regenerate not just its tail but also limbs, organs, and even parts of its brain — without scarring. Scientists study it intensively for regenerative medicine.

questions.question: What is the fastest animal in the world in a dive?
questions.fun_fact: The peregrine falcon reaches speeds over 380 km/h in a dive — faster than a high-speed train. Special bony tubercles in its nostrils deflect airflow so it can breathe at those speeds.

questions.question: Which jellyfish is theoretically immortal?
questions.fun_fact: Turritopsis dohrnii can reverse its life cycle and transform from a mature adult back into a polyp — again and again. It is the only known biologically immortal animal.

questions.question: How many species of beetles are estimated to exist on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: With around 400,000 known species, beetles are the most species-rich order in the animal kingdom. Biologist J.B.S. Haldane reportedly said the Creator had 'an inordinate fondness for beetles'.

questions.question: Which animal eats its own brain?
questions.fun_fact: The sea squirt swims as a larva and has a simple brain. Once it attaches to a surface, it digests its own brain and nervous system because it no longer needs them.

questions.question: Which animal can survive the longest without water?
questions.fun_fact: The kangaroo rat can live its entire life without drinking a single drop of water. It extracts all moisture from metabolising dry seeds and has extremely efficient kidneys.

questions.question: Which plant folds its leaves when touched?
questions.fun_fact: The mimosa folds its leaves within seconds of being touched. Remarkably, it can learn: after repeated harmless stimulation it stops responding — a form of memory without a brain.

questions.question: How many brains (ganglia) does a leech have?
questions.fun_fact: A leech has 32 ganglia, each functioning as a mini-brain. It also has 3 jaws, around 300 teeth, and a complex digestive tract with multiple paired caeca for storing blood meals.

questions.question: Which animal sleeps up to 22 hours a day?
questions.fun_fact: Koalas sleep up to 22 hours a day because eucalyptus leaves are extremely low in nutrients and require a lot of energy to digest. Their caecum, at 2 metres, is the longest relative to body size of any mammal.

questions.question: Which fish can climb trees on land?
questions.fun_fact: The climbing perch (Anabas testudineus) can crawl on land using its gill covers and fins, and can even climb trees. It breathes atmospheric air through a special labyrinth organ.

questions.question: How long does it take a plastic bottle to decompose in nature?
questions.fun_fact: A PET bottle takes around 450 years to decompose, breaking down into ever-smaller microplastics but never truly disappearing. Only about 9% of all plastic ever produced has been recycled.

questions.question: Which animal can generate electric shocks of up to 860 volts to stun prey?
questions.fun_fact: The electric eel can generate shocks of up to 860 volts — enough to stun a horse. It is not actually an eel but a knifefish more closely related to catfish.

questions.question: Which animal has the largest eye in the animal kingdom?
questions.fun_fact: The eyes of the colossal squid can be up to 27 cm in diameter — the size of a football. This allows it to detect the faint bioluminescence of sperm whales in the deep ocean.

questions.question: Which creature has more nerve cells in its arms than in its brain?
questions.fun_fact: Two thirds of an octopus's 500 million neurons are in its arms, not its brain. Each arm can taste, feel, and make decisions independently — even severed arms react for several minutes.

questions.question: Which mammal is one of the very few that lays eggs instead of giving birth?
questions.fun_fact: The platypus is a monotreme — a mammal that lays eggs. Males also have venomous spurs on their hind legs powerful enough to kill a small dog and cause humans excruciating pain that morphine barely dulls.

questions.question: What is the long spiral 'tusk' of the narwhal actually made of?
questions.fun_fact: The narwhal's 'tusk' is a single canine tooth that grows straight through the upper lip and can reach 3 metres. It is riddled with about ten million nerve endings, letting the whale taste salinity and temperature through it.

questions.question: Which mammal is famously resistant to cancer and barely ages?
questions.fun_fact: Naked mole rats live up to 30 years — ten times longer than similar-sized rodents — and almost never develop cancer. Their cells produce an unusually heavy form of hyaluronan that prevents tumour growth.

questions.question: Which is the only mammal covered in keratin scales?
questions.fun_fact: Pangolins are the only mammals with true scales made of keratin — the same material as human fingernails. When threatened they roll into a tight ball that even lions struggle to open.

questions.question: Why do bats almost always hang upside down to rest?

answers.text: Their leg tendons lock passively under their own weight
Hanging keeps their wing membranes warm

questions.fun_fact: A bat's foot tendons are arranged so its own body weight clamps the talons shut — it costs zero muscular effort to hang. A sleeping bat that dies in this pose can stay attached to the ceiling indefinitely.

questions.question: Which marine mammal is the closest living relative of the elephant?
questions.fun_fact: Manatees and dugongs share a common ancestor with elephants from around 50 million years ago. Like elephants, they grow tusks and replace their molars in a slow-moving conveyor belt throughout life.

questions.question: Vampire bats are known for which unusual social behaviour?

answers.text: Regurgitating blood to feed roost-mates that didn't find food

questions.fun_fact: Vampire bats starve within about 70 hours, so they share blood meals by regurgitation — and remember who returned the favour. They form long-term 'friendships' and prefer to share with bats that previously shared with them.

questions.question: Why does a sloth's fur often look green?

answers.text: Algae live in tiny grooves in each hair
Pigment from their diet of leaves

questions.fun_fact: Each sloth hair has microscopic cracks that hold rainwater, and algae grow inside them. The greenish coat camouflages the sloth in the canopy and is even home to moths found nowhere else.

questions.question: Why does a beaver's front teeth appear bright orange?
questions.fun_fact: Beaver incisors have iron-rich enamel that is harder than ordinary tooth enamel and resists acid better. Researchers studied the structure to design tougher human dental fillings.

questions.question: Which large mammal's vocalisations include calls so low that humans cannot hear them?
questions.fun_fact: Blue whale calls dip below 20 Hz — beneath human hearing — yet are so loud (up to 188 decibels) that they can travel for hundreds of kilometres through deep ocean sound channels.

questions.question: Which animal has an eye bigger than its brain?
questions.fun_fact: An ostrich eyeball is roughly 5 cm across — larger than its walnut-sized brain. The huge eye, the biggest of any land animal, lets the bird spot predators from kilometres away on the savanna.

questions.question: How do male Gentoo penguins typically court a female?

answers.text: By presenting her with a smooth pebble
By offering a freshly caught fish
By performing a long underwater dive

questions.fun_fact: Gentoo males hunt for the smoothest pebble they can find and lay it at the female's feet. Accepted pebbles go into the nest — and females have been observed stealing prized stones from rivals' nests.

questions.question: How far can an owl rotate its head?
questions.fun_fact: Owls turn their heads up to about 270° because their eyes are fixed tubes in the skull and cannot swivel. Extra neck vertebrae and special blood-vessel reservoirs keep the brain supplied during the twist.

questions.question: Compared to its body, which bird lays the largest egg of any species?
questions.fun_fact: A kiwi egg can weigh nearly a quarter of the mother's body weight — proportionally six times larger than a chicken's egg. X-rays of pregnant kiwis show the egg occupying almost the entire abdomen.

questions.question: Why are flamingos pink?

answers.text: Pigments from the algae and shrimp they eat
A pigment they synthesise in their liver

questions.fun_fact: Flamingos hatch grey-white and turn pink from beta-carotene pigments in algae and brine shrimp. Captive flamingos fed a plain diet fade to pale grey — zoos add carotenoids to keep them showy.

questions.question: What stops a woodpecker from giving itself brain damage while hammering?

answers.text: A spongy bone structure and a hyoid bone that wraps around the skull
An extra-thick layer of fluid around the brain
They pause between strikes long enough for shock to dissipate

questions.fun_fact: A woodpecker's skull contains spongy plate-like bone and a long elastic hyoid that loops over the cranium like a seat belt, distributing impact. Strikes can hit 1,200 g of deceleration — enough to concuss most animals.

questions.question: Which family of birds has been shown to manufacture and customise tools?
questions.fun_fact: New Caledonian crows bend twigs into hooks and trim leaf edges into barbed probes — different shapes for different jobs. They also pass tool-making techniques on to their young, a form of culture.

questions.question: How does the common swift manage to sleep during its long migrations?

answers.text: It dozes briefly while still flying
It clings to cliffs at night
It rests on the ocean surface

questions.fun_fact: Tracking studies show common swifts can stay airborne for up to 10 months without landing, gliding in slow circles at altitude to catch micro-sleeps. They eat, drink, mate and sleep on the wing.

questions.question: Which living bird has the longest wingspan?
questions.fun_fact: A wandering albatross can stretch its wings to 3.5 metres. A specialised shoulder-locking tendon holds the wings open with almost no muscle effort, so the bird can glide for hours without a single flap.

questions.question: How long can a chameleon's tongue be relative to its body?

answers.text: Up to about twice its body length
Up to five times its body length

questions.fun_fact: Small chameleon species can shoot their tongue out to roughly twice their body length in about 1/16 of a second, accelerating faster than a fighter jet. A sticky mucus tip glues prey on contact.

questions.question: How does a snake manage to swallow prey wider than its own head?

answers.text: Its lower jaw halves are connected by a stretchy ligament, not fused
It dislocates and re-locates its jaw with each meal
It chews the prey into smaller pieces first

questions.fun_fact: The two halves of a snake's lower jaw are joined by an elastic ligament that lets them spread sideways. The jaw never actually dislocates — the popular myth is wrong, but the stretch is dramatic enough to swallow a deer in some pythons.

questions.question: How does the wood frog survive a North American winter?

answers.text: It burrows deep below the frost line
It freezes solid and thaws back to life

questions.fun_fact: The wood frog stops its heart and lets up to 65% of its body water turn to ice. Glucose pumped into its cells acts as antifreeze, and in spring it simply thaws and hops away — sometimes within an hour of warming.

questions.question: What distinctive feature gives the glass frog its name?

answers.text: You can see its beating heart through the skin of its belly
Its eggs are translucent like marbles
Its bones glow faintly under moonlight

questions.fun_fact: Glass frogs have transparent ventral skin that reveals the heart, liver and digestive tract. When they sleep, they hide most of their red blood cells in the liver, making them up to 60% more see-through.

questions.question: What is unusual about the male of most deep-sea anglerfish species?

answers.text: He permanently fuses to the female and becomes a sperm-producing appendage
He guards thousands of eggs alone for months
He glows brighter than the female to attract her

questions.fun_fact: In many anglerfish species the tiny male bites into the much larger female and stays attached for life, their tissues merging until he is little more than a sperm gland. He receives nutrients directly from her bloodstream.

questions.question: Which animal can strike its prey with the acceleration of a small-calibre bullet?
questions.fun_fact: A peacock mantis shrimp's club-like appendage accelerates underwater at over 10,000 g, smashing snail shells and even cracking aquarium glass. The strike is so fast the surrounding water briefly boils into vapour bubbles.

questions.question: Where does most of the fine white sand on a tropical coral beach actually come from?

answers.text: It is excreted by parrotfish that bite and grind coral
It is eroded directly from offshore cliffs
It is dust blown in from inland deserts

questions.fun_fact: A single large parrotfish can produce several hundred kilograms of coral sand per year by chewing coral, digesting the algae and excreting the rest. Much of a Maldives beach is, technically, parrotfish poo.

questions.question: How does the archerfish catch insects above the water?

answers.text: It spits a precisely aimed jet of water
It leaps out and snatches them mid-air
It lures them with bioluminescent flashes

questions.fun_fact: Archerfish shoot water jets up to 2 metres and compensate for light refraction at the water surface — a calculation that takes humans years of physics. Young fish learn to aim by watching the adults.

questions.question: Which gland in a snake's mouth is the evolutionary source of its venom?
questions.fun_fact: Venom in snakes evolved from ordinary salivary glands — proteins meant for digestion became weapons. The same molecular toolkit also gave rise to venom in lizards like the Komodo dragon.

questions.question: Where do salmon use Earth's magnetic field?

answers.text: To find the exact river of their birth when returning to spawn
To stay upright in fast currents

questions.fun_fact: Salmon imprint on the unique magnetic signature of their natal river and use it years later to return from thousands of kilometres at sea. Iron-containing cells in their nose act as a built-in compass.

questions.question: How long does a typical adult mayfly live after it emerges from the water?
questions.fun_fact: Adult mayflies of many species live less than 24 hours — some species only a few minutes — and don't even have a working mouth. They live for years as aquatic nymphs and emerge only to mate.

questions.question: Which predator has roughly a 95% success rate when hunting?
questions.fun_fact: Dragonflies catch up to 95% of the prey they target, far better than lions (~25%) or sharks. Their independently moving compound eyes and predictive flight neurons let them intercept rather than chase.

questions.question: Which microscopic animal can survive boiling, freezing, radiation and even the vacuum of space?
questions.fun_fact: Tardigrades survive by drying into a 'tun' state with less than 3% water and a protective protein that turns their cells into glass-like solids. Live tardigrades were recovered after exposure to open space in 2007.

questions.question: How many colour-receiving cone types does a mantis shrimp's eye have?
questions.fun_fact: Mantis shrimp eyes carry 12 to 16 types of photoreceptors. Counter-intuitively, behavioural tests suggest they discriminate colours less finely than humans — but each receptor works as a fast spectral channel, like onboard hardware.

questions.question: Through which body part does a butterfly taste?

answers.text: The tip of its proboscis only

questions.fun_fact: Butterflies have taste sensors on their feet, so they 'taste' a leaf the moment they land. Females use this to identify the exact plant species their caterpillars can eat before laying eggs.

questions.question: What is the relationship between many ant species and aphids?

answers.text: The ants protect aphids and 'milk' them for sugary honeydew
The ants are parasitised by aphid larvae
The ants prey on aphids as their main food

questions.fun_fact: Some ants herd aphids like livestock, carrying them to fresh plants and defending them from ladybirds. In return the ants stroke the aphids with their antennae to trigger droplets of sugary honeydew.

questions.question: How do African termite mounds keep their interior at a stable temperature?

answers.text: Internal chimneys drive passive air convection
Worker termites fan their wings constantly

questions.fun_fact: Macrotermes mounds use a network of chimneys and side vents that pulls cool air in through the base and pushes warm air out the top — a passive design that inspired Zimbabwe's Eastgate Centre, which uses 90% less air-conditioning.

questions.question: Which animal is estimated to have the most teeth — over 20,000 on a microscopic 'tongue'?
questions.fun_fact: A garden snail's radula is a ribbon-like tongue covered in thousands of microscopic teeth used to rasp food. Limpets have an even tougher version — their teeth are made of the strongest known biological material, stronger than spider silk.

questions.question: What unusual problem-solving ability has the slime mould Physarum polycephalum been shown to have?

answers.text: It can find the shortest path through a maze without a brain
It can recognise individual human faces
It can navigate by the position of the sun

questions.fun_fact: In a famous 2010 experiment, slime mould placed on a map of Japan grew connections between food stacks that closely matched the actual Tokyo rail network — without neurons, eyes or any central control.

questions.question: Why do periodical cicadas emerge after exactly 13 or 17 years rather than, say, 12 or 15?

answers.text: Prime-number cycles make it harder for predators to synchronise
These are the only cycles their sap-feeding can sustain

questions.fun_fact: 13 and 17 are prime numbers, so any predator whose population peaks every 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 years can rarely align with a cicada emergence. The trick lets billions of cicadas appear at once and overwhelm anything that eats them.

questions.question: Pando in Utah, often called the largest known organism by mass, is what kind of life form?

answers.text: A single clonal colony of quaking aspen trees
An underground network of fungal hyphae

questions.fun_fact: Pando looks like a forest of 47,000 aspens but is actually one organism sharing a single root system, weighing about 6,000 tonnes. Some estimates put its age at thousands of years.

questions.question: Which everyday fruit is mildly radioactive thanks to its high potassium content?
questions.fun_fact: Bananas contain potassium-40, a naturally radioactive isotope. The dose is so tiny it's harmless, but the 'banana equivalent dose' is a tongue-in-cheek unit used to explain radiation risks to the public.

questions.question: Why did the rediscovery of the Wollemi pine in 1994 cause such a sensation?

answers.text: It was known only from 90-million-year-old fossils
Its bark contains a powerful natural pesticide

questions.fun_fact: The Wollemi pine was thought extinct since the time of the dinosaurs until a hiker stumbled on a few dozen trees in a remote Australian canyon. The exact location is kept secret, and saplings are now sold worldwide.

questions.question: Why does the corpse flower smell so strongly of rotting meat when it blooms?

answers.text: It mimics carrion to attract flies and beetles for pollination
It is digesting trapped insects inside its bloom
It uses the smell to repel grazing animals

questions.fun_fact: Amorphophallus titanum can stand 3 metres tall and warms its bloom to body temperature to broadcast the stench of rotting flesh, drawing carrion flies. It blooms unpredictably, sometimes only once a decade.

questions.question: How does the dodder plant (Cuscuta) feed itself?

answers.text: It wraps around other plants and taps into their sap with rootlike haustoria
It catches insects with sticky pads
It absorbs nutrients only from rainwater

questions.fun_fact: Dodder has almost no chlorophyll and survives by stealing water and nutrients from host plants. Seedlings can even 'sniff out' nearby tomato plants and grow toward the scent, ignoring less tasty neighbours.

questions.question: How many true leaves does the desert plant Welwitschia mirabilis produce in its entire lifetime?

answers.text: Roughly one new leaf per year

questions.fun_fact: Welwitschia grows just two strap-like leaves that keep extending and tattering for the plant's entire life — which can last over 1,500 years in the Namib Desert. It is the only living member of its plant family.

questions.question: Why can a mature giant sequoia survive most forest fires unharmed?

answers.text: Its thick fibrous bark is highly fire-resistant
It pumps water down its trunk when smoke appears
Its leaves release a flame-retardant gas

questions.fun_fact: Sequoia bark can be over 60 cm thick and is laced with tannins and almost no resin, so it chars rather than burns. Sequoias actually depend on fire: the heat opens their cones and clears competing plants for seedlings.

questions.question: How do mangrove trees deal with the salt in seawater?

answers.text: They filter most salt at the roots and excrete the rest from special leaf glands
They store all salt in fruit that drops into the sea
They convert it into oxygen through photosynthesis

questions.fun_fact: Mangrove roots act as ultrafilters that block up to 97% of salt. Whatever sneaks through is concentrated in older leaves or pushed out via salt-secreting glands — visible as tiny crystals on the leaf surface.

questions.question: What kind of organism is a lichen?

answers.text: A partnership between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium
An ancient lineage of land-dwelling sponges

questions.fun_fact: Lichens are a stable symbiosis: the fungus builds the body, the photosynthetic partner provides sugars. The combination is so tough that lichens were the first organisms shown to survive exposure to outer space.

questions.question: What is the so-called 'wood wide web' that connects most forest trees?

answers.text: Underground networks of mycorrhizal fungi linking tree roots
Airborne pheromones released by leaves under attack
Electrical signals travelling through interlocking branches

questions.fun_fact: Mycorrhizal fungi wrap around tree roots and trade nutrients for sugars, but they also link different trees underground. Experiments tracked carbon flowing from large 'mother trees' to younger seedlings through this fungal web.

questions.question: Where on Earth has it essentially never rained on record in some weather stations?
questions.fun_fact: Parts of the Atacama have weather stations that have never registered measurable rainfall. NASA tests Mars rovers there because the soil is so dry and lifeless it serves as the closest earthly analogue of the Red Planet.

questions.question: What's odd about the Sailing Stones of Death Valley's Racetrack Playa?

answers.text: They slide across the flat lakebed and leave long trails
They emit a faint hum at sunset
They are perfectly round and identical in size

questions.fun_fact: The rocks drift for hundreds of metres, leaving grooves no one ever sees them make. Time-lapse cameras in 2014 finally caught the trick: thin sheets of winter ice break up and gentle winds push the floating ice — and the rocks frozen into it — across the mud.

questions.question: Why does Antarctica's 'Blood Falls' flow bright red?

answers.text: Iron-rich brine from beneath the glacier oxidises in the air
Red algae bloom in the meltwater each summer
Volcanic ash stains the ice below the surface

questions.fun_fact: Trapped under Taylor Glacier is a salty, iron-rich lake cut off from sunlight for over a million years. When the brine seeps out and meets oxygen, the iron rusts on contact and paints the ice a vivid blood-red.

questions.question: What happens to most animals that fall into Tanzania's Lake Natron?

answers.text: They become calcified and 'mummified' by the lake's chemistry
They are rapidly digested by piranha-like fish

questions.fun_fact: Lake Natron's water is alkaline enough to burn skin and saturated with sodium carbonate. Dead birds and bats washed ashore are coated in salts and harden into eerie stone-like statues — yet the lake is also the breeding ground for nearly all of Africa's lesser flamingos.

questions.question: What causes the glowing blue 'sea sparkle' sometimes seen in waves at night?
questions.fun_fact: Dinoflagellates such as Noctiluca scintillans emit a brief blue flash when jostled — a startle response that may attract bigger predators to eat whatever is disturbing them. Dense blooms can make every footprint glow.

questions.question: Roughly how many lightning strikes hit the Earth every second?
questions.fun_fact: Satellites count around 8 million lightning strikes a day — roughly 100 per second worldwide. The single most lightning-prone spot is Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, where storms light up the sky almost every night.

questions.question: Why do the methane lakes of Russia's Yamal Peninsula sometimes form spectacular ice bubbles?

answers.text: Methane from decomposing plants is trapped under the freezing surface
Cosmic rays ionise the water as it freezes
Reindeer migrations stir the lakebed mud

questions.fun_fact: Microbes in the lake sediment turn dead plants into methane. The gas rises in plumes and gets trapped as the surface freezes, stacking up into ghostly white discs. Punch a hole, hold a flame, and you can ignite a column of fire.

questions.question: What causes 'fairy circles' — almost perfect bare-earth rings in some African grasslands?

answers.text: Likely competition between grass roots for scarce water

questions.fun_fact: Fairy circles in the Namib are still debated, but the leading explanation is that grasses self-organise into rings to share scarce rainwater — neighbours drink the centre dry while the ring keeps moisture for itself. Termite-based theories survive as runners-up.

questions.question: What is a 'snow roller', a phenomenon occasionally spotted in open fields?

answers.text: A natural snowball formed when wind pushes wet snow across the ground
A type of high-altitude lenticular cloud
A spinning column of ice crystals during a blizzard

questions.fun_fact: Snow rollers form only when wet, sticky snow sits on a slick base layer and steady wind nudges chunks along. They roll up into hollow cylinders that can grow taller than a bicycle wheel — and then collapse the moment you touch them.
